activities.caption: pair each of the five questions with what it asks
activities.name: ahQuestionsMatch

config.prompt: Art historians ask the same five questions of every work — match question to ask:

pairs.right: what was happening in that society when the work was made
what ideas, objects and materials travelled to make it possible
what the object is made of, and what that making made possible
who paid for it, who looked at it, and what it was for
what the work has meant to people since

config.why: Five questions, a checklist for meeting a stranger: where did they grow up, who did they know, what are they made of, what work did they do, what have people said since?

activities.caption: bet first — who answered the Council of Trent?
activities.name: ahTrentPredict

config.q: The Council of Trent (1563) ruled that religious images should teach clearly and move the viewer. Whose work answers that brief most literally?
choices: Caravaggio — violent spotlights, ordinary models, saints with dirty feet
Jan van Eyck — luminous oil glazes on panel
config.why: Baroque realism as recruitment: the Counter-Reformation demanded persuasion, and Caravaggio delivered it in spotlight and dirt.

activities.anchor: made for a paying civic client rather than an altar
activities.caption: fill the blanks — a new audience invents itself
activities.name: ahDutchCloze

config.text: Rembrandt's Night Watch (%%0%%) is a militia group portrait turned into moving theatre — light as storytelling, painted for the %%1%% Republic's merchants, with no %%2%% commission at all.
config.hint: A year, a republic, and the patron that isn't there.

activities.anchor: They are how the objects got made
activities.caption: file the travellers — what kind of thing crossed the border?
activities.name: ahTravelBuckets

config.prompt: Nothing on the timeline is culturally self-made. File what travelled:

items.label: ultramarine ground from lapis lazuli, mined in one Afghan valley
oil paint perfected in Flanders, travelling south within a generation
Japonisme — flat colour, cropped views, expressive line
African and Iberian carvings behind the Demoiselles' masks
the silver of Potosí funding Spanish churches

config.why: Interactions are not a footnote — they are how the objects got made. The colonial dimension runs through the whole story, both ways.

activities.anchor: belongs to the story of interactions across cultures
activities.caption: bet first — why Italy switched to oil
activities.name: ahOilPredict

config.q: Why did Italian painters adopt van Eyck's oil medium within a generation of its arrival?
choices: Tempera's drying speed made sfumato and luminous glaze-building impossible
Oil was cheaper than egg yolk
config.why: Oil dries slowly and can be reworked — the technique that invented revision, glazes and the Mona Lisa's sfumato.

activities.caption: rebuild the medium timeline — each shift has an enabler
activities.name: ahMediumOrder

config.prompt: Put the technical enablers in order:
items: Egg tempera — crisp icons, dry in minutes
Photography announced (1839) — likeness taken from painting
Paint in collapsible tubes (Rand, 1841) — the studio leaves the building
Impression, Sunrise (1872) — minutes at a harbour window
config.why: Tempera forced crispness, oil allowed revision, the camera pushed painting to ask what only painting could do, and the tube freed it from the studio. Materials are ideas.

activities.anchor: one day's plaster, one day's painting
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the fresco trade-off
activities.name: ahFrescoSpot

config.prompt: One line of this fresco answer is wrong — click it:
lines: Fresco means painting pigment into wet plaster.
Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling — over 5,000 square feet of it — was built from giornate.
Each giornata was one day's plaster and one day's painting.
The method's advantage: yesterday's section can be reworked like oil, at leisure.
config.correction: Fresco has a HARD DEADLINE — pigment into wet plaster cannot be reworked; yesterday's section is finished forever.
config.why: Fresco bought permanence at the price of revisability — the exact opposite trade from oil, which is why the two media carry different kinds of ambition.

activities.caption: call the gap — tube to harbour window
activities.name: ahTubeEstimate

config.prompt: Rand patented the collapsible paint tube in 1841; Monet painted Impression, Sunrise in minutes at a harbour window in 1872. Roughly how many years apart are the two?
config.why: 1872 − 1841 = 31 years from the tube to the harbour window — industrialised materials made Impressionism physically possible.
config.context: And the critic Leroy's mockery — 'Impressionists' — became the movement's name.

activities.anchor: a slow-motion conversation conducted at the speed of light
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the lag grows with distance
activities.name: asLightCloze

config.text: One AU is 149.6 million km, and light takes %%0%% minutes %%1%% seconds to cross it. Neptune is over four light-%%2%% away; Voyager 1's radio commands take nearly %%3%% days for the round trip.
config.hint: The Sun you see is always 8 minutes old — and the lag only grows.

activities.caption: place Mercury on the period curve
activities.name: asMercuryPlace

config.prompt: Every planet sits on the Kepler curve. Place Mercury's orbital period on the scale (days):
config.why: 88 days at 0.39 AU — the nearest dot on the curve. Neptune takes 165 years; one power law holds everywhere between.
config.context: Discovered in 1619 from naked-eye data; it survived Newton, relativity and 5,000+ exoplanet discoveries.

activities.anchor: the first credible number for the scale of the solar system
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the yardstick itself
activities.name: asAuEstimate

config.prompt: Cassini and Richer's 1672 parallax landed within about 7% of the truth. Roughly how many million km is the astronomical unit?
config.why: 149.6 million km — measured first by parallax from Paris and Cayenne, 7,000 km apart, after two millennia of Greek estimates running twenty times too small.
config.context: The transits of Venus (1761, 1769) then shrank the error to about 1% — Cook sailed to Tahiti for the second.

activities.anchor: The map still has blank edges
activities.caption: file the residents — who lives where in the system?
activities.name: asTourBuckets

config.prompt: Rock, nothing, gas, ice, nothing. File each resident:

items.label: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — within 1.5 AU
Uranus and Neptune at 19 and 30 AU
the asteroid belt at 2–3 AU — under 4% of our Moon's mass
the Kuiper Belt, including Pluto and Eris
the Oort Cloud's trillion comet nuclei, never directly observed

config.why: The geography is relentlessly repetitive — and a thousand times past Neptune, the Oort Cloud is inferred entirely from the orbits of long-period comets.

config.q: Shrink the Sun to a 22 cm football. How big does Earth become, and where does it orbit?
choices: A 2 mm peppercorn, orbiting 23 metres away
A 2 cm ball, orbiting 2 metres away
config.why: Peppercorn Earth at 23 m; Jupiter a marble at 120 m; Neptune 700 m out — and Proxima Centauri is another football 6,300 km away. No version that fits in a room shows the planets as anything but specks.

activities.caption: true or false — the true-scale system
activities.name: asSpeckJudge

statements.s: All eight planets together hold under 0.2% of the solar system's mass.
statements.why: The Sun holds the other 99.8%+ — the planets are specks by mass as well as size.

statements.s: The classroom poster with planets shoulder to shoulder shows their order and nothing else.
statements.why: At true scale, every planet would be invisible without a microscope.

statements.s: The asteroid belt's combined mass exceeds our Moon's.
statements.why: Under 4% of it — a failed planet kept from forming by Jupiter's bullying.

statements.s: The Oort Cloud has been directly observed.
statements.why: Inferred entirely from the orbits of long-period comets falling sunward from random directions.

activities.caption: pair each region with what its receipt says
activities.name: asReceiptMatch

config.prompt: Every world is a receipt from the young disk's shopping trip:

pairs.right: only rock and metal condense: small, dense worlds

pairs.left: past the frost line (~3 AU) — cold
pairs.right: ices freeze; embryos bulk up and grab hydrogen — gas giants
slower growth — the partially formed ice giants

config.why: The rocky-inner/gassy-outer split is the signature of formation — not an accident of taste.
